WHY DOES THE SHUTTLE ROLL JUST AFTER LIFTOFF?
The following answer and translation are provided by Ken Jenks
(kjenks@gothamcity.jsc.nasa.gov).
The ""Ascent Guidance and Flight Control Training Manual
""During the vertical rise phase
commanded until an I-loaded V(rel) sufficient to assure launch tower
clearance is achieved. Then
orients the vehicle to a heads down attitude required to generate a
negative q-alpha
column2: which in turn alleviates structural loading. Other

This really is a good answer
column2: but it's couched in NASA jargon. I'll try

column1: to interpret.
1)	We wait until the Shuttle clears the tower before rolling.
2)	Then
column2: we roll the Shuttle around so that the angle of attack

column1: between the wind caused by passage through the atmosphere (the
""relative wind"") and the chord of the wings (the imaginary line
between the leading edge and the trailing edge) is a slightly
negative angle (""a negative q-alpha"").	This causes a little bit of
""downward"" force (toward the belly of the Orbiter
direction) and this force ""alleviates structural loading.""
We have to be careful about those wings -- they're about the
most ""delicate"" part of the vehicle.
3)	The new attitude (after the roll) also allows us to carry more
mass to orbit
column2: or to achieve a higher orbit with the same mass

column1: to change the orbit to a higher or lower inclination than would be
the case if we didn't roll (""performance gain"").
4)	The new attitude allows the crew to fly a less complicated
flight path if they had to execute one of the more dangerous abort
maneuvers
column2: the Return To Launch Site (""decreased abort maneuver

column1: complexity"").
5)	The new attitude improves the ability for ground-based radio
antennae to have a good line-of-sight signal with the S-band radio
antennae on the Orbiter (""improved S-band look angles"").
6)	The new attitude allows the crew to see the horizon
helpful (but not mandatory) part of piloting any flying machine.
7)	The new attitude orients the Shuttle so that the body is
more nearly parallel with the ground
column2: and the nose to the east

column1: (usually).  This allows the thrust from the engines to add velocity
in the correct direction to eventually achieve orbit.  Remember:
velocity is a vector quantity made of both speed and direction.
The Shuttle has to have a large horizontal component to its
velocity and a very small vertical component to attain orbit.

Here is a computation I did a long time ago that computes the length
of the daylight.  You should be able to convert the information here
to sunrise and sunset times.
Rouben Rostamian                          Telephone: 410-455-2458
Department of Mathematics and Statistics  e-mail:
University of Maryland Baltimore County   bitnet: rostamian@umbc.bitnet
Baltimore
Definitions:
z = the tilt of the axis of the planet away from the normal to its
orbital plane.  In case of the Earth z is about 23.5 degrees
I do not recall the exact value.  In case of Uranus
90 degrees.
u = latitude of the location where the length of the day is measured.
Paris is at about 45 degrees.  North pole is at 90.
a = angular position of the planet around the sun.  As a goes from
0 to 360 degrees
column2: the planet makes a full circle around the sun.

column1: The spring equinox occurs at a=0.
L = daylight fraction = (duration of daylight)/(duration of a full day).
On the equator (u=0) L is always 1/2.  Near the north pole (u=90 degrees)
L is sometimes one and sometimes zero
column2: depending on the time of the year.

column1: Computation:
Define the auxiliary angles p and q by:
sin p = sin a sin z
cos q = h ( tan u tan p )
Conclusion:
L = q / 180   (if q is measured in degrees)
L = q / pi    (if q is measured in radians)
Wait!  But what is h?
The cutoff function h is defined as follows:
h (s) = s    if  |s| < 1
= 1    if   s > 1
As an interesting exercise
column2: plot L versus a.   The graph will shows

column1: how the length of the daylight varies with the time of the year.

concave / self intersecting polygons.
This efficiency can largely be attributed to the fact that
simple convex polygons only have a left and a right edge on each scan line.
Complex (figure 8 type polygons) can be a bit trickier.
The less than N sides specification especially if it is a very small
number like 3 or 4 allow othe optimisations to be made.
Thus for a high speed game application I think you are looking for
code that exploits and is hence limited to drawing simple convex
polygons.

14) How to tell whether a point is within a planar polygon.
Consider a ray originating at the point of interest and continuing to
infinity.  If it crosses an odd number of polygon edges along the way
the point is within the polygon.  If the ray crosses an even number of
edges
column2: the point is either outside the polygon

column1: hole formed from intersecting polygon edges.  This idea is known in
the trade as the Jordan curve theorem; see Eric Haines' article in
Glassner's ray tracing book (above) for more information
treatment of special cases.
Another method is to sum the absolute angles from the point to all
the vertices on the polygon.  If the sum is 2 pi
if the sum is 0 the point is outside.  However
order of magnitude slower than the previous method because evaluating the
trigonometric functions is usually quite costly.
Code for both methods (plus barycentric triangle testing) can be found in
the Ray Tracing News
pub/Graphics/RTNews/RTNv5n3.Z.

This problem has now been solved. Tests on people with one normal eye and one
affected eye have shown that there is an axis for each type of disorder onto
which all the colours collapse. For protanopes this joins up 473nm and 574nm on
the spectral locus (the edge of the horseshoe); for deuteranopes the line is
very similar
*So* to convert colours from normal vision to a simulated protanopia or
duuteranopia:
1) Plot the colour on a uniform chromaticity diagram
2) Construct a line from this point to the appropriate confusion point
3) Find the intersection of this line with the appropriate axis line
4) This is the new chromaticity.
The best reference for this is Meyer
defective vision and computer graphics displays'
Applications 8(5) 28-40.
You will also need a decent reference on basic colour science if you are not
familiar with the CIE XYZ colour model and the uniform chromaticity scale diagram.

OTIS is here for the purpose of distributing original artwork

The basic idea behind ""digital immortality"" is that computer networks
are here to stay and that anything interesting you deposit on them
will be around near-forever.  The GIFs and JPGs of today will be the

formats

intersect).  This was done so that in the future

water jugs.  In the early testing fragments of the plastic

[1]  What is JPEG?
JPEG (pronounced ""jay-peg"") is a standardized image compression mechanism.
JPEG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group
committee that wrote the standard.  JPEG is designed for compressing either
full-color or gray-scale digital images of ""natural""
It does not work so well on non-realistic images
drawings.
JPEG does not handle black-and-white (1-bit-per-pixel) images
handle motion picture compression.  Standards for compressing those types
of images are being worked on by other committees
respectively.
JPEG is ""lossy""
column2: meaning that the image you get out of decompression isn't

column1: quite identical to what you originally put in.  The algorithm achieves much
of its compression by exploiting known limitations of the human eye
the fact that small color details aren't perceived as well as small details
of light-and-dark.  Thus
column2: JPEG is intended for compressing images that will

column1: be looked at by humans.  If you plan to machine-analyze your images
small errors introduced by JPEG may be a problem for you
invisible to the eye.
A useful property of JPEG is that the degree of lossiness can be varied by
adjusting compression parameters.  This means that the image maker can trade
off file size against output image quality.  You can make *extremely* small
files if you don't mind poor quality; this is useful for indexing image
archives
aren't happy with the output quality at the default compression setting
can jack up the quality until you are satisfied
[2]  Why use JPEG?
There are two good reasons: to make your image files smaller
24-bit-per-pixel color data instead of 8-bit-per-pixel data.
Making image files smaller is a big win for transmitting files across
networks and for archiving libraries of images.  Being able to compress a
2 Mbyte full-color file down to 100 Kbytes or so makes a big difference in
disk space and transmission time!  (If you are comparing GIF and JPEG
size ratio is more like four to one.  More details below.)
If your viewing software doesn't support JPEG directly
convert JPEG to some other format for viewing or manipulating images.  Even
with a JPEG-capable viewer
column2: it takes longer to decode and view a JPEG image

column1: than to view an image of a simpler format (GIF
JPEG is essentially a time/space tradeoff: you give up some time in order to
store or transmit an image more cheaply.
It's worth noting that when network or phone transmission is involved
time savings from transferring a shorter file can be much greater than the
extra time to decompress the file.  I'll let you do the arithmetic yourself.
The other reason why JPEG will gradually replace GIF as a standard Usenet
posting format is that JPEG can store full color information: 24 bits/pixel
(16 million colors) instead of 8 or less (256 or fewer colors).  If you have
only 8-bit display hardware then this may not seem like much of an advantage
to you.  Within a couple of years
column3: 8-bit GIF will look as obsolete as

column1: black-and-white MacPaint format does today.  Furthermore
in section 7
column2: JPEG is far more useful than GIF for exchanging images among

column1: people with widely varying color display hardware.  Hence JPEG is considerably
more appropriate than GIF for use as a Usenet posting standard.

the meaning of these settings.  ""Quality 95"" does NOT mean ""keep 95% of the
information""

[7]  What's all this hoopla about color quantization?
Most people don't have full-color (24 bit per pixel) display hardware.
Typical display hardware stores 8 or fewer bits per pixel
256 or fewer distinct colors at a time.  To display a full-color image
computer must map the image into an appropriate set of representative
colors.  This process is called ""color quantization"".  (This is something
of a misnomer
column2: ""color selection"" would be a better term.  We're stuck with

column1: the standard usage though.)
Clearly
column2: color quantization is a lossy process.  It turns out that for most

column1: images
column2: the details of the color quantization algorithm have MUCH more impact

column1: on the final image quality than do any errors introduced by JPEG (except at
the very lowest JPEG quality settings).
Since JPEG is a full-color format
column2: converting a color JPEG image for display

column1: on 8-bit-or-less hardware requires color quantization.  This is true for
*all* color JPEGs: even if you feed a 256-or-less-color GIF into JPEG
comes out of the decompressor is *not* 256 colors
This happens because JPEG's lossiness affects each pixel a little
differently
column2: so two pixels that started with identical colors will probably

column1: come out with slightly different colors.  Each original color gets ""smeared""
into a group of nearby colors.  Therefore quantization is always required to
display a color JPEG on a colormapped display
source.  The only way to avoid quantization is to ask for gray-scale output.
(Incidentally
column2: because of this effect it's nearly meaningless to talk about

column1: the number of colors used by a JPEG image.  Even if you attempted to count
the number of distinct pixel values
column2: different JPEG decoders would give you

column1: different results because of roundoff error differences.  I occasionally see
posted images described as ""256-color JPEG"".  This tells me that the poster
(a) hasn't read this FAQ and (b) probably converted the JPEG from a GIF.
JPEGs can be classified as color or gray-scale (just like photographs)
number of colors just isn't a useful concept for JPEG.)
On the other hand
column2: a GIF image by definition has already been quantized to

column1: 256 or fewer colors.  (A GIF *does* have a definite number of colors in its
palette
column2: and the format doesn't allow more than 256 palette entries.)

what you can display
image quality than if you had quantized once from a full-color image.

Why do we need gamma correction at all ?
Gamma correction is needed because of the nature of CRTs (cathode
ray tubes - the monitors usually used for viewing images). If you
have some sort of real live scene and turn it into a computer
image by measuring the amount of light coming from each point of
the scene
column2: then you have created a ""linear"" or un-gamma-corrected

column1: image. This is a good thing in many ways because you can manipulate
the image as if the values in the image file were light (ie. adding
and multiplying will work just like real light in the real world).
Now if you take the image file and turn each pixel value into a voltage
and feed it into a CRT
column2: you find that the CRT _doesn't_ give you

column1: an amount of light proportional to the voltage. The amount of light
coming from the phosphor in the screen depends on the the voltage
something like this:
Light_out = voltage ^ crt_gamma
So if you just dump your nice linear image out to a CRT
will look much too dark. To fix this up you have to ""gamma correct""
the image first. You need to do the opposite of what the CRT
will do to the image
what you want. So you have to do this to your image:
gamma_corrected_image = image ^ (1/crt_gamma)

I didn't want to mess with tga or rle.  So I wrote the following script.
All you need is the very standard set of pbm utilities.
This script is a .pov to .jpg converter.  Just run it like this:
pov2jpg 1280 1024 fred.pov
You will need to modify the path's in the script to reflect where you put
povray and its include files.  If you have a problem with disk space
can use named pipes instead of temporary files.
I hope you find it useful...
#!/bin/sh
if [ $# -lt 3 ] ; then
echo ""usage:  $0 width height sourcefile.pov other_options""
exit
fi
width=$1
height=$2
datafile=$3
shift 3
#basedatafile=`echo $datafile | sed -e ""s/\(.*\)\.pov/\1/""`
thedatafile=`basename $datafile`
basedatafile=`basename $datafile .pov`
dirdatafile=`dirname $datafile`
cd $dirdatafile
/afs/rnd.sas.com/u/sherman/pov/povsrc/build/povray \
+l/afs/rnd.sas.com/u/sherman/pov/povscn/include \
+o/tmp/data$$ +w${width} +h${height} +fr +i${thedatafile} $*
echo "" ""
rawtopgm $width $height < /tmp/data$$.grn > /tmp/green$$
rawtopgm $width $height < /tmp/data$$.red > /tmp/red$$
rawtopgm $width $height < /tmp/data$$.blu > /tmp/blue$$
rgb3toppm /tmp/red$$ /tmp/green$$ /tmp/blue$$ | cjpeg > ${basedatafile}.jpg
rm /tmp/red$$ /tmp/green$$ /tmp/blue$$ /tmp/data$$.grn /tmp/data$$.red \
/tmp/data$$.blu
echo ""Wrote output to ${basedatafile}.jpg""

I have been studying the problem of font conversion for a few years but
have never had the need to implement such a system. Well
opportunity to write some font rendering software so I would like to have
some of my questions answered before I jump into the deep end.
The main problem I face is how to use the even/odd or non-winding rules to
turn the outlines into a single outline polygon (my renderer can handle
complex polygons so there is no need to reduce the polygons to simple
polygons). For example
column2: in the letter ""O"" there are two outlines:

column1: 1) The outside outline which is clockwise (TrueType font)
2) The inside outline which is counterclockwise.
One common solution used by a number of rendering packages is to simply
connect the inner outline to the outer outline at the point where the
two outlines are closest. This is equivalent to descibing a ""polygon with
holes"". The renderer will then make the appropriate hole since the interior
polygon edges are in the opposite direction to the outside edges.
I do not want to use this simplistic system since:
1) It will not handle all outline fonts properly (it is not a simple
matter to connect the outer outline to the inner outline for
some fancy fonts).
2) It does not properly handle the even/odd or non-winding rules.
From my research over the years the proper solution is to use a trapezoid
decomposition algorithm to scan convert the outlines into trapezoids (as
is done by the Postscript and TrueType font rasterizers). These trapezoidal
polygons can then be easily and properly rendered by the 3D scanline renderer.
My question is: are there any better solutions to turning the outlines into
polgyons other than the trapezoid decomposer? I am not fond of this solution
since it creates excess number of polygons.
Another question
column2: for those in the know: what is the best algorithm to create

column1: bevelled and/or offset curves for font outlines? I have a dozen papers on these
subjects but I can't tell which method is the best to implement.

True immersive visualization (VR)
column2: requires the rendering of complex visual

column1: databases at anywhere from 20 to 60 newly rendered frames per second.  This
is a similar requirement to that of traditional flight simulators for pilot
training. If the frame rate is too low
column2: the user notices the stepping of

column1: the frames as they move their head rapidly around the scene
of the graphics is not smooth and contiguous.  Thus the graphics system
must be powerful enough to sustain high frame rates while rendering complex
data representations.

column2: the frame rate must be constant.  If the system renders 15

column1: frames per second at one point
column2: then 60 frames per second the next (perhaps

column1: due to the scene in the new viewing direction being simpler than what was
visible before)
column2: the user can get heavily distracted by the medium (the

column1: graphics computer) rather than focusing on the data. To maintain a constant
frame rate
column2: the system must be able to run in real-time.  UNIX in general

column1: does not support real-time operation
column2: but Silicon Graphics has modified the

column1: UNIX kernel for its multi-processor systems to be able to support real-time

by Dave Watson
Each pair of tetrahedral vertices define a plane which is a
perpendicular bisector of the line between that pair.  Express each
plane in the form Ax + By + Cz = D
and solve the set of simultaneous equations from any three of those
planes that have a vertex in common (all vertices are used).
The solution is the circumcenter.

of moving bodies (commonly called Special Relativity) with Reimanian
geometry.  The result was the General Theory of Relativity
it's most noteworthy strengths is that it accounts for the precession

[1]  What is JPEG?
JPEG (pronounced ""jay-peg"") is a standardized image compression mechanism.
JPEG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group
committee that wrote the standard.  JPEG is designed for compressing either
full-color or gray-scale digital images of ""natural""
It does not work so well on non-realistic images
drawings.
JPEG does not handle black-and-white (1-bit-per-pixel) images
handle motion picture compression.  Standards for compressing those types

respectively.
JPEG is ""lossy""

the fact that small color details aren't perceived as well as small details

column2: JPEG is intended for compressing images that will

column1: be looked at by humans.  If you plan to machine-analyze your images

invisible to the eye.
A useful property of JPEG is that the degree of lossiness can be varied by

archives

[2]  Why use JPEG?
There are two good reasons: to make your image files smaller
24-bit-per-pixel color data instead of 8-bit-per-pixel data.
Making image files smaller is a big win for transmitting files across
networks and for archiving libraries of images.  Being able to compress a
2 Mbyte full-color file down to 100 Kbytes or so makes a big difference in
disk space and transmission time!  (If you are comparing GIF and JPEG
size ratio is more like four to one.  More details below.)

convert JPEG to some other format for viewing or manipulating images.  Even

[7]  What's all this hoopla about color quantization?
Most people don't have full-color (24 bit per pixel) display hardware.
Typical display hardware stores 8 or fewer bits per pixel
256 or fewer distinct colors at a time.  To display a full-color image
computer must map the image into an appropriate set of representative
colors.  This process is called ""color quantization"".  (This is something
of a misnomer
column2: ""color selection"" would be a better term.  We're stuck with

column1: the standard usage though.)
Clearly
column2: color quantization is a lossy process.  It turns out that for most

column1: images
column2: the details of the color quantization algorithm have MUCH more impact

column1: on the final image quality than do any errors introduced by JPEG (except at
the very lowest JPEG quality settings).
Since JPEG is a full-color format
column2: converting a color JPEG image for display

column1: on 8-bit-or-less hardware requires color quantization.  This is true for
*all* color JPEGs: even if you feed a 256-or-less-color GIF into JPEG
comes out of the decompressor is *not* 256 colors
This happens because JPEG's lossiness affects each pixel a little
differently
column2: so two pixels that started with identical colors will probably

column1: come out with slightly different colors.  Each original color gets ""smeared""
into a group of nearby colors.  Therefore quantization is always required to
display a color JPEG on a colormapped display
source.  The only way to avoid quantization is to ask for gray-scale output.
(Incidentally
column2: because of this effect it's nearly meaningless to talk about

column1: the number of colors used by a JPEG image.  Even if you attempted to count
the number of distinct pixel values
column2: different JPEG decoders would give you

column1: different results because of roundoff error differences.  I occasionally see
posted images described as ""256-color JPEG"".  This tells me that the poster
(a) hasn't read this FAQ and (b) probably converted the JPEG from a GIF.
JPEGs can be classified as color or gray-scale (just like photographs)
number of colors just isn't a useful concept for JPEG.)
On the other hand
column2: a GIF image by definition has already been quantized to

column1: 256 or fewer colors.  (A GIF *does* have a definite number of colors in its
palette
column2: and the format doesn't allow more than 256 palette entries.)

column1: For purposes of Usenet picture distribution
column2: GIF has the advantage that the

column1: sender precomputes the color quantization
This is also the *disadvantage* of GIF: you're stuck with the sender's
quantization.  If the sender quantized to a different number of colors than
what you can display
image quality than if you had quantized once from a full-color image.
Furthermore

But there is always a judgement call based on pastoral considerations.
Each pastor makes his own decisions (it isn't a church-wide conspiracy
against participation).  The Palm Sunday liturgy
blessing and distribution of the palms and procession
getting long before you get to the Passion; some pastors feel that they
should not make the people stand through that long narrative.  Also
orchestrated proclamation with multiple readers and public participation
in the crowd quotations runs longer than the single-reader proclamation
--- in churches with multiple Masses for the Sunday
necessary to go with the briefer options just to ""get 'em in and get 'em
out"".
Each parish is different.  Catholics are no longer canonically tied to
their geographic parishes.  It is possible that another Catholic parish
in the Columbus area (based on the Ohio State address) has a liturgy
closer to your preferences.  Or talk to some of your fellow
parishioners and see how common your preferences are --- pastors
generally ARE willing to listen to non-confrontational requests.  Though
you probably should bring along a paramedic in case he reacts too strongly
to the shock of people asked for a _longer_ Sunday Mass.
Perhaps the problem is that recent liturgical development hasn't follow
the continuous evolution model (the accumulation of small changes
single one of which is too hard to take) but rather the punctuated
equilibrium model (things stay the same and we get accustomed to them
then the marked mutation hits).  {My apologies if I am mis-remembering
the names of the evolutionary theories.}"

devices.  Most implementations support the X Window System and take
advantage of a 3D extension to X called ""PEX"".  PEXlib is a slightly
lower"" level API which was designed to efficiently support the PEX
extension to X.
Some advantages of using PEXlib...
- Integrates with Xlib
- Provides immediate mode capabilities
- Is free of ""policy""
- PEX supports PHIGS
column2: but is currently being extended to support

column1: features not found in PHIGS (like texture mapping
PEXlib will give you access to all of these features.
Some advantages of using PHIGS...
- Support for multiple devices
- Support for archiving
- PHIGS has predefined input devices to make input easier
- PHIGS can handle exposure events and resizing for you
- PHIGS can help you with colormap selection/creation.
